name: Bathsheba
interpretive_note: 2 Samuel 11 gives Bathsheba almost no voice or interiority in the initial encounter with David — 'he sent messengers, and took her.' Interpreters differ over how much agency the text implies she had in a situation where a reigning king summoned a subject's wife: some read the episode as mutual sin, others emphasize the severe power imbalance and read David's action as closer to abuse of royal authority than to a two-sided affair, noting that Nathan's parable names David alone as the guilty 'rich man' (2 Samuel 12:1-6) and that 2 Samuel 11:27 states plainly that 'the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD' without naming Bathsheba's culpability. Scripture does not state her intent, and this site does not pick a side.
source_summary: Wife of Uriah the Hittite, summoned by King David while her husband was at war; after David arranged Uriah's death to cover the resulting pregnancy, she became David's wife and, decades later, successfully secured the throne for her son Solomon against a rival claimant.
family_friendly_summary: Bathsheba went through something very painful — King David saw her, and made choices that hurt her deeply and led to the death of her husband, a loyal soldier named Uriah. Even though what happened wasn't Bathsheba's fault, it changed the course of her life. Later, God still blessed her: her son Solomon became Israel's next great king, and Bathsheba herself helped make sure Solomon actually received the throne when others tried to take it first. Bathsheba is remembered in the Bible as an important part of the family line that eventually led to Jesus. Bathsheba's story shows that God can bring good purposes out of even the most painful situations in our lives.
adult_story: While her husband Uriah, one of David's elite warriors, was at war, David saw Bathsheba bathing, sent for her, and she came; when she conceived, David recalled Uriah to sleep with his wife to cover it up, and when Uriah refused out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, David had him killed in battle (2 Samuel 11:2-21). Scripture assigns the moral verdict plainly and only to David: 'the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD' (2 Samuel 11:27). On learning of Uriah's death, Bathsheba mourned him, and only afterward was she brought into David's house as a wife (2 Samuel 11:26-27). The prophet Nathan confronted David with a parable in which David alone is condemned; God's judgment included the death of the child born from the affair (2 Samuel 12:1-19). Their second son was Solomon, given the name Jedidiah, 'beloved of the LORD,' by Nathan — grace following judgment (2 Samuel 12:24-25). Decades later, with David old and Adonijah moving to seize the throne, Bathsheba acts decisively: at Nathan's urging, she reminds David of his oath that Solomon would reign, securing his public confirmation before he died (1 Kings 1:11-31). After Solomon's coronation, Bathsheba appears again as queen mother, carrying a request from Adonijah that Solomon reads as a renewed threat and answers by executing him (1 Kings 2:13-25). Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names her, pointedly, as 'the wife of Uriah' (Matthew 1:6) — grace, not respectability, shaping the Messiah's ancestry.
